questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\left(\sqrt[3]{x + \sqrt{2 - x^2}}\right)\left(\sqrt[6]{1 - x\sqrt{2 - x^2}}\right)}{\sqrt[3]{1 - x^2}}\,dx; \, (x \in (0, 1)) =$
questions.solution:
Let the given integral be $I = \int \dfrac{(x + \sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/3} (1 - x\sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/6}}{(1 - x^2)^{1/3}} \, dx$.

Consider the first term in the numerator. We can rewrite it by squaring the expression inside and changing the exponent:

$(x + \sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/3} = \left((x + \sqrt{2 - x^2})^2\right)^{1/6}$

Expanding the square, we get:

$(x + \sqrt{2 - x^2})^2 = x^2 + (2 - x^2) + 2x\sqrt{2 - x^2} = 2 + 2x\sqrt{2 - x^2} = 2(1 + x\sqrt{2 - x^2})$

Substituting this back, the first term becomes:

$(x + \sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/3} = 2^{1/6} (1 + x\sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/6}$

Now, multiply this with the second term in the numerator:

Numerator $= 2^{1/6} (1 + x\sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/6} (1 - x\sqrt{2 - x^2})^{1/6}$

Using the identity $(a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2$, we get:

Numerator $= 2^{1/6} \left(1 - x^2(2 - x^2)\right)^{1/6}$

Numerator $= 2^{1/6} (1 - 2x^2 + x^4)^{1/6}$

Numerator $= 2^{1/6} \left((1 - x^2)^2\right)^{1/6}$

Since $x \in (0, 1)$, $1 - x^2 \gt 0$, so this simplifies to:

Numerator $= 2^{1/6} (1 - x^2)^{1/3}$

Substituting the simplified numerator back into the integral:

$I = \int \dfrac{2^{1/6} (1 - x^2)^{1/3}}{(1 - x^2)^{1/3}} \, dx$

$I = \int 2^{1/6} \, dx$

$I = 2^{1/6}x + c$

Answer: $2^{\dfrac{1}{6}}x + c$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{(1 - x^2)}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{(1 + x^2)^3}}\,dx = \alpha\dfrac{x^{\beta}}{(1 + x^2)^{\gamma}} + C; \, \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ and $C$ is constant of integration, then $\alpha : \beta : \gamma$ will be
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{1 - x^2}{\sqrt{x}(1 + x^2)^{3/2}} \,dx$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $x^2$, we get:

$I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{x^2} - 1}{\dfrac{\sqrt{x}(1 + x^2)^{3/2}}{x^2}} \,dx$

$I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{x^2} - 1}{\left(\dfrac{1 + x^2}{x}\right)^{3/2}} \,dx = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{x^2} - 1}{\left(x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{3/2}} \,dx$

Let $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = t$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$:

$\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) \,dx = dt \Rightarrow \left(\dfrac{1}{x^2} - 1\right) \,dx = -dt$

Substituting this into the integral:

$I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{-dt}{t^{3/2}} = -\displaystyle\int t^{-3/2} \,dt$

$I = -\left(\dfrac{t^{-1/2}}{-1/2}\right) + C = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{t}} + C$

Substituting back $t = \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x}$:

$I = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x}}} + C = 2\dfrac{x^{1/2}}{(1 + x^2)^{1/2}} + C$

Comparing this with the given expression $\alpha\dfrac{x^{\beta}}{(1 + x^2)^{\gamma}} + C$, we get:

$\alpha = 2$, $\beta = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the ratio is:

$\alpha : \beta : \gamma = 2 : \dfrac{1}{2} : \dfrac{1}{2} = 4 : 1 : 1$

Answer: $4 : 1 : 1$

questions.q: If \(\int \frac{d x}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-3)}=\frac{1}{k} \log _e\left\{\frac{|x-3|^3|x+1|}{(x-2)^4}\right\}+c\), then the value of \(k\) is
questions.solution:
Hint: \(\int \frac{d x}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-3)}=\int\left(\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{(x-2)}+\frac{C}{x-3}\right) d x\)
\(\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-3)}=\frac{A(x-2)(x-3)+B(x+1)(x-3)+C(x+1)(x-2)}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-3)} \\
& \Rightarrow 1=A(x-2)(x-3)+B(x+1)(x-3)+C(x+1)(x-2) \\
& \text { for } x=-1 \\
& 1=A(-3)(-4) \Rightarrow A=\frac{1}{12} \\
& \text { for } x=2 \\
& 1=B(3)(-1) \Rightarrow B=-\frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}\)
\(\text { for } x=3\)
\(\begin{aligned} & 1=C(4)(1) \Rightarrow C=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \therefore I=\frac{1}{12} \int \frac{1}{x+1} d x-\frac{1}{3} \int \frac{1}{x-2} d x+\frac{1}{4} \int \frac{1}{x-3} d x \\ & =\frac{1}{12} \ln |x+1|-\frac{1}{3} \ln |x-2|+\frac{1}{4} \ln |x-3|+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12}\left[\ln |x+1|-\ln |x-2|^4+\ln |x-3|^3\right]+C \\ & =\frac{1}{12} \ln \frac{(|x+1|)(|x-3|)^3}{(x-2)^4}-C \\ & \therefore k=12\end{aligned}\)

Let $I=\int \cos \left(2 \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\right\} d x$
Put $x=\cos 2 \theta \Rightarrow d x=-2 \sin 2 \theta d \theta\begin{aligned} \therefore I &=\int \cos \left(2 \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1-\cos 2 \theta}{1+\cos 2 \theta}}\right\}(-2 \sin 2 \theta) d \theta \\ &=-2 \int \cos \left\{2 \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{2 \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 \cos ^{2} \theta}}\right\} \sin 2 \theta d \theta \\ &=-2 \int \cos \left(2 \tan ^{-1}(\tan \theta) \sin 2 \theta d \theta\right.\\ &=-2 \int \cos 2 \theta \sin 2 \theta d \theta \\ &=\int \cos 2 \theta d(\cos 2 \theta) \\ &=\frac{\cos ^{2} 2 \theta}{2}+C \\ &=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C \end{aligned}$

If $\int e^{\sin x} \cdot\left[\frac{x \cos ^{3} x-\sin x}{\cos ^{2} x}\right] d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+c$
where c is constant of integration, then $f(x)$ is
equal to
questions.solution: We have. $\int e^{\operatorname{cin} x}\left(\frac{x \cos ^{3} x-\sin x}{\cos ^{2} x}\right) d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+c\int e^{\operatorname{sin} x}(x \cos x-\sec x \tan x) d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+c\int e^{\operatorname{sin} x}(x \cos x-1+1-\sec x \tan x) d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+c\left.\int[ e^{\sin x} \cos x(x-\sec x)+e^{\sin x}(1-\sec x \tan x)\right] d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+c\int \frac{d}{d x}\left\{e^{\sin x}(x-\sec x)\right\} d x=e^{\sin x} f(x)+ce^{\operatorname{cin} x}(x-\sec x)=e^{\sin x} f(x)+cf(x)=x-\sec x$

If $\int f(x) \sin x \cos x d x=\frac{1}{2\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right)} \log f(x)+c$
where $c$ is the constant of integration, then $f(x)$ is equal to
questions.solution: We have. $\int f(x) \sin x \cos x d x=\frac{1}{2 b^{2}-a^{2}} \log (f(x))+c\Rightarrow f(x) \sin x \cos x=\frac{1}{\left.2 b^{2}-a^{2}\right)} \cdot \frac{1}{f(x)} \cdot f'(x)\Rightarrow \quad f(x) \sin 2 x=\frac{1}{b^{2}-a^{2}} \cdot \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\Rightarrow \quad \sin 2 x=\frac{1}{b^{2}-a^{2}} \frac{f(x)}{(f(x))^{2}}\Rightarrow \quad \int \sin 2 x d x=\frac{1}{b^{2}-a^{2}} \int \frac{f(x)}{(f(x))^{2}} d x\Rightarrow \quad \frac{-\cos 2 x}{2}=\frac{1}{b^{2}-a^{2}} \cdot\left(\frac{-1}{f(x)}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \quad \frac{\cos 2 x\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right)}{2}=\frac{1}{f(x)}\Rightarrow \quad f(x)=\frac{2}{\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right) \cos 2 x}$

questions.q: $\int \cos (\log x) d x=F(x)+C,$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Here, $F(x)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $I=\int \cos (\log x) d x$
Put $\log x=t\Rightarrow \quad x=e^{t}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad d x &=e^{t} d t \\ \therefore \quad I &=\int e^{t} \cos t d t \\ &=\frac{e^{t}}{1^{2}+1^{2}}[\cos t+\sin t]+C \end{aligned}\left[\because \int e^{a x} \cos b x d x=\frac{e^{a x}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}[a \cos b x+b \sin b x]+c\right]\Rightarrow \quad I=\frac{e^{t}}{2}[\cos t+\sin t]+C\quad \quad=\frac{x}{2}[\cos (\log x)+\sin (\log x]+C\therefore f(x)=\frac{x}{2}[\cos (\log x)+\sin (\log x)]$

questions.solution:

\begin{array}{l}
=\int \frac{d x}{(x-2)^{-1 / 3}(x+3)^{7 / 3}} \\

questions.q: A family of curves is such that the length intercepted on the $y$ -axis between the origin and the tangent at a point is three times the ordinate of the point of contact. The family of curves is
questions.solution:
Let the general equation of tangent.
Which passes through the point $(x, y)$ is 
$(Y-y)=\frac{d y}{d x}(x-x)\Rightarrow \quad Y-y=X \frac{d y}{d x}-x \frac{d y}{d x}$
for length of $Y$ -intercept, put $X=0$ in Eq. $(1),$ we get $Y-y=-x \frac{d y}{d x}\Rightarrow \quad Y=y-x \frac{d y}{d x}$
Now,according to the guestion Y-intercept $=3 \times$ ordinate of the point of contact $\Rightarrow \quad y-x \frac{d y}{d x}=3 y\Rightarrow \quad-x \frac{d y}{d x}=2 y\Rightarrow\int \frac{d y}{y}=-\int \frac{2 d x}{x}$ (on integrating)
$\Rightarrow \quad \log y=-2 \log x+\log C\Rightarrow \quad \log y+\log x^{2}=\log C\Rightarrow y x^{2}=C$. where $C$ is a constant.

questions.q: The solution of the differential equation $y \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right) d x=\left\{x \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-y\right\} d y \quad$ satisfying $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1 \mathrm{is}$
questions.solution:
Given differential equation is

\begin{array}{l}
y \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right) d x=\left\{x \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-y\right\} d y \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{x \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-y}{y \sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}=\frac{x}{y}-\frac{1}{\sin \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}
\end{array}

On putting $v=\frac{x}{y} \Rightarrow x=y\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x}{d y}=v \cdot 1+y \frac{d v}{d y}$ in Eq. $0 .$ we get
$v+y \frac{d v}{d y}=v-\frac{1}{\sin v}\Rightarrow \quad y \frac{d v}{d y}=-\frac{1}{\sin v}\Rightarrow \quad-\int \sin v d v=\int \frac{d y}{y}$
(on integrating)
$\Rightarrow \quad \cos v=\log y+C\Rightarrow \quad \cos \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=\log y+C$
Given at $x=\frac{\pi}{4}, y=1$ then from $\mathrm{Eq}$. (i) $\Rightarrow \quad \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\log (1)+C\Rightarrow \quad\left(C=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
On putting the value of $C$ in Eq. (0), we get $\cos \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=\log _{e} y+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
Which is the required solution. So option D is correct.
